title: Ghazals of longing
hookLine: his Persian love-poems to the Divine are still sung in gurdwaras

lines: A LOVE SONG, SUNG TO GOD.
cards: In a gurdwara, the ragis sit with harmonium and tabla, and sing the Guru's own word from the Guru Granth Sahib. Then, now and then, the words change color. The language turns Persian.
The tune softens. And the song is a love song, sung to God, by someone who sounds as if he can hardly bear the distance. Those songs were written by the poet we met two days ago.

teach.b: A ghazal is a love poem with a shape of its own. The form began in Arabic and flowered in Persian. It's built from couplets, pairs of lines, and each couplet is complete in itself, like a bead.
String the beads together and you have the ghazal.
By custom, the poet signs the poem near the end, slipping his pen name into the last couplet. So in Bhai Nand Lal's ghazals, you'll hear him name himself: Goya.
His ghazals are gathered in a collection known as the Divan-e-Goya. And what are they about? Longing.
The lover and the Beloved. The ache of distance, the sweetness of a glance, the lover who would give anything for one meeting. That's the old language of the Persian ghazal, and Nand Lal draws on it.
But in his poems the Beloved is the Divine, and the face the heart turns toward is the One, seen through the Guru. Hold three things together. First, the form.
Each couplet stands alone, so a ragi can sing one, or several, and each still makes sense. Second, the feeling. Some people picture devotion as duty, a list of things to do.
Nand Lal's ghazals sound more like someone who's simply in love, and can't hide it. Third, the place. These Persian love songs aren't kept on a library shelf.
They're sung in gurdwaras, in kirtan, in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikh custom welcomes them there.
So a Persian love form found a home in the Guru's house, and it came in singing.

how: Ragis sing Bhai Nand Lal's Persian ghazals in kirtan in gurdwaras, alongside the Guru's bani, and Sikhs also read them in Persian and in translation.

o: a chant repeating one name of God many times
a long ballad of stanzas telling a Guru's life
a love poem of couplets, signed with a pen name

games.q: you're Nand Lal, finishing a ghazal. by the custom of the form, what goes into the last couplet?
games.why: by custom, the ghazal poet signs his pen name in the last couplet. Nand Lal's ghazals carry the name Goya.

practice: If you can, play a few minutes of a ghazal of Bhai Nand Lal sung in kirtan; if not, sit with the idea of one, a single couplet, complete in itself, sung slowly to someone you love.
Don't try to understand every word: notice where the music lifts and where it waits, and if you pray, let Waheguru rise in you along with the tune.

wordCard.voice: Ghazal. A love poem built from couplets, as Persian poets shaped it, signed with the poet's pen name. Bhai Nand Lal's ghazals, signed Goya, are love songs to the Divine.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, via Persian from Arabic: a ghazal, a love poem in couplets.

carryVoice: Your line: love, in persian. Couplets like beads, strung for the Beloved. See you tomorrow.
